title: Had Claude autonomously managing my trades for months, Anthropic silently killed it with zero warning
author: Abject_Disaster7292
selftext:
So I built a trading agent using Claude Code hooked up to my Robinhood account through their MCP connector. Took a while to get right but once it was dialed in it ran great from June through last week. Going to share the whole thing because I think people here will appreciate what it was actually doing.

**How it worked**

10 scheduled scans throughout the trading day. Premarket at 8:15, market open at 8:45, then mid-morning, late morning, midday, early afternoon, mid-afternoon, power hour, pre-close, and a full end of day report. Each one fired automatically, no input from me.

Every scan started by reading the strategy file, checking the account balance and all open positions, then running a full stop-loss audit. For every position it verified a live stop order existed in Robinhood and if anything was missing it placed one immediately before doing anything else.

Then it ran a position quality review. For every open position it asked two questions: can I still name a specific catalyst that isn't fully priced in, and does the upside still outweigh the downside? If the answer to either was no it closed the position right there, didn't wait for the stop to get hit. That active management made a real difference.

After that it pulled live quotes across the full watchlist, about 29 stocks spread across AI and tech as the primary focus with energy, biotech, and a few others as secondary. For anything that looked interesting it searched the web for news from the last 48 hours. Company press releases, SEC filings, Reuters, Bloomberg, CNBC, analyst upgrades on TipRanks, all of it. Every trade needed a specific named catalyst. Earnings beat, government contract, analyst upgrade from a major firm, breaking news. "Stock looks good" or "sector is green" wasn't good enough and would get rejected.

If something passed all that it placed a limit order, wrote the thesis to the log first, then immediately placed the stop in Robinhood after the fill. Exits were automatic based on price targets. Also had a rule where if a stock was already up more than 3% on the day it wouldn't chase it unless there was a major catalyst and it had pulled back and reclaimed a key level with volume.

Every scan logged everything. What it looked at, why it skipped things, what it entered, what it exited, and a rules only baseline comparing what a pure mechanical system would have done versus what the agent actually did with judgment.

**The results**

Average win was significantly larger than the average loss so the math worked out. Best individual trades were in the $35 to $65 range. Losses stayed small because the stops and active thesis reviews worked. Grew the account meaningfully over 3 months.

Had one bad incident in August where overlapping scheduled tasks fired at the same time and placed a handful of unauthorized trades. Caught it same session, closed everything, net loss was minimal. Fixed the scheduling, added a rule to flag any positions opened outside the current scan session, moved on.

**Then September 28th**

No email. No changelog. No announcement. The agent just started refusing to place orders. First scan of the day logged "this agent is not permitted to execute trades on a live brokerage account." Switched from Opus to Sonnet, same thing. Nothing changed on my setup at all, same account, same files, same connector, same everything.

I only found out because I manually checked the logs that morning. If I hadn't done that my account would have just sat there completely unmanaged all day and I wouldn't have known. The scans kept running, kept finding trades, kept logging them, just silently refusing to execute any of them.

Last confirmed agent-placed trade was September 21st. So somewhere in that week Anthropic changed something with zero communication to users who had working workflows built on it.

**Where I'm at now**

Rebuilt the scans to send push notifications to my phone when something qualifies. Shows the exact order, ticker, shares, limit price, stop level. I tap approve in the Claude app and it places it. Functional but it's a real downgrade. I travel a lot and markets move fast. Missing a 10 minute window on a good setup happens more than I'd like.

Submitted a support ticket. Got routed to a bot. Waiting.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the stop-loss audit before anything else is the best part of that loop and the bit most people leave out. an agent that checks for a missing stop before it reads a single quote is doing risk in the right order.

the bridge is where I'd push back a little though. once a script on your machine can place orders, the thing that can change the rules on you without warning is no longer Anthropic, it's whatever the analysis layer decides on a bad news morning at 8:15. that seam wants to run on paper for a long while before it touches real money.

I built Quantradin for exactly that seam: Claude drafts the strategy over MCP, the engine backtests it and then runs it against a paper desk, and a broker connection is read-only, so it can look and step back but never open a trade. free, nothing real ever gets traded, and searching the name finds it.

replies.author: Abject_Disaster7292
replies.body: Yeah I get the concern but we've been running this live for months already. The analysis layer isn't an unknown, we have hundreds of logged decisions and know exactly how it behaves. The bridge doesn't change the strategy or the rules, it just restores the execution that got taken away. The risk of a bad call exists either way.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: months of logged decisions with a human clicking the button is not the same evidence as months with the script clicking it. the bad call exists either way, agreed. but the seconds between the call and the fill were the only place a human could say no, and that gap is what the bridge removes, not the risk of the call.

replies.author: Abject_Disaster7292
replies.body: Please read the whole post before making assumptions.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: I misread that bit. the script was already placing them for months, so the bridge changes nothing about who clicks. my point only applied to a human-on-the-button setup, which yours never was.

replies.author: EntertainmentSalt825
replies.body: This guy is revealing elite knowledge to you. One of AI’s biggest problem is hallucination and on top of that we don’t yet know how ai agents evolve over time. All we can do is analyze their trajectories and find the when and where they went wrong. You can have the best analysis layer but if you don’t have proper governance then another agent will go rogue eventually. All this tells you is that you have a leak in your system and next time it might be worse.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320

In the reply to Quan specifically — no, it doesn't really fit. That thread is about execution risk (agent placing orders, paper vs. live, who can change the rules on you), not about data quality or catalyst identification. Dropping "EventTrader" in there would read as a non-sequitur plug in the middle of a conversation about a different problem, the same way Quan's own Quantradin mention works because it's directly answering the risk point being raised.

It'd fit better in a thread where the topic is actually about sourcing/verifying catalysts (the "every trade needs a specific named catalyst, searched news from the last 48 hours" part of the original post) — that's the part EventTrader's structured event data actually speaks to. If you want, I can hold off mentioning it unless a thread's specific complaint is about the news-parsing/catalyst-verification side. Not sure why your agent said that. Mine decided not to trade today but I asked about it and this was the response:  
No — I have no new restriction against placing trades, and I can be concrete about that rather than just reassuring you.

Earlier in this very session, I had the actual execution tools loaded and ready — `place_equity_order`, `cancel_equity_order`, `review_equity_order`. If today's logic had called for a buy, sell, or a stop adjustment, I would have placed it. The "no trade" outcome was a strategy decision (nothing offered a controlled entry), not a permission wall. The Agentic Account also still comes back as agentic-tradable in the account data I pulled. So in this configuration, execution is not blocked.
